papers.title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus
papers.abstract: Abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever. One Sentence Summary A bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing Lassa virus GPC and NP confers robust protection against lethal Lassa virus infection

papers.source_body_en: Abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. papers.title: A transgenic Syrian hamster model for New World hemorrhagic fever mammarenavirus infection
papers.abstract: Mammarenaviruses are endemic in rodent populations worldwide, and their zoonotic transmission can lead to a severe, life-threatening hemorrhagic fever (HF) syndrome. In the Americas, five New World mammarenaviruses (NWMs) are known to cause HF. As vaccines and antiviral therapy options are limited, these viruses pose a significant public health risk and a threat to national security. Research into NWM pathogenesis and the development of effective countermeasures is restricted by the shortage of small-animal models that faithfully reproduce human disease. The pathogenic NWMs use human transferrin receptor 1 (hTfR1) as the receptor for cellular entry. Here, we describe the development of an hTfR1 knock-in golden Syrian hamster line and its susceptibility to Junín virus (JUNV) infection. This transgenic hamster infection model supports TfR1-mediated entry as an essential step in JUNV pathogenesis and provides a novel small-animal model to advance the development of promising host receptor-directed therapies and direct-acting antivirals to improve outcomes in patients with severe disease caused by pathogenic NWMs.

elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges the limitations of using a non-human model and the need for further validation in human-relevant contexts.

papers.title_zh: 新世界出血热乳腺病毒感染的转基因叙利亚仓鼠模型
papers.source_body_en: Mammarenaviruses are endemic in rodent populations worldwide, and their zoonotic transmission can lead to a severe, life-threatening hemorrhagic fever (HF) syndrome. In the Americas, five New World mammarenaviruses (NWMs) are known to cause HF. As vaccines and antiviral therapy options are limited, these viruses pose a significant public health risk and a threat to national security. Research into NWM pathogenesis and the development of effective countermeasures is restricted by the shortage of small-animal models that faithfully reproduce human disease. The pathogenic NWMs use human transferrin receptor 1 (hTfR1) as the receptor for cellular entry. Here, we describe the development of an hTfR1 knock-in golden Syrian hamster line and its susceptibility to Junín virus (JUNV) infection. This transgenic hamster infection model supports TfR1-mediated entry as an essential step in JUNV pathogenesis and provides a novel small-animal model to advance the development of promising host receptor-directed therapies and direct-acting antivirals to improve outcomes in patients with severe disease caused by pathogenic NWMs.

papers.full_text: Co-Infection of Lassa Fever-Malaria (LF) in Endemic Settings: Influence on LF Case Detection in Health Facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria Abstract: In malaria-endemic settings, a positive malaria result may explain fever while Lassa fever (LF) remains clinically possible. This study assessed LF-malaria co-infection, probable missed LF suspicion, and diagnostic delays in selected health facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria. A convergent mixed-methods design combined retrospective review of 463 LF and malaria records from 2021 – 2023 across 10 purposively selected facilities in five high-burden LGAs with nine key-informant interviews. Co-infection required positive LF and malaria laboratory results. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and logistic regression; qualitative findings were analysed thematically and integrated through a joint display. All 463 records were purposefully selected as confirmed LF cases. Of these, 297 (64.1%) had positive LF and malaria results. Malaria was suspected in 440 (95.0%) records, and 324 (70.0%) had prior malaria treatment. Probable missed LF suspicion occurred in 103 (22.2%) records. Malaria positivity was associated with missed suspicion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.30, 95% CI 2.13–13.19; p < 0.001). Interviews highlighted symptom overlap, malaria-first reasoning, treatment failure, restricted RT-PCR access, specimen-transport barriers, notification gaps and uneven refresher training. Overall, 386 (83.4%) patients recovered and 53 (11.4%) died; the case-fatality proportion among confirmed LF records was 11.4%. In this selected sample, malaria appeared to mask LF rather than establish an independent cause of mortality. Malaria confirmation should not close the LF detection pathway. Parallel assessment, timely LF specimen collection, reliable transport, effective surveillance communication and practical diagnostic algorithms may support earlier detection. References: [1]. full_text_sections.full_text: Co-Infection of Lassa Fever-Malaria (LF) in Endemic Settings: Influence on LF Case Detection in Health Facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria Abstract: In malaria-endemic settings, a positive malaria result may explain fever while Lassa fever (LF) remains clinically possible. This study assessed LF-malaria co-infection, probable missed LF suspicion, and diagnostic delays in selected health facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria. A convergent mixed-methods design combined retrospective review of 463 LF and malaria records from 2021 – 2023 across 10 purposively selected facilities in five high-burden LGAs with nine key-informant interviews. Co-infection required positive LF and malaria laboratory results. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and logistic regression; qualitative findings were analysed thematically and integrated through a joint display. All 463 records were purposefully selected as confirmed LF cases. Of these, 297 (64.1%) had positive LF and malaria results. Malaria was suspected in 440 (95.0%) records, and 324 (70.0%) had prior malaria treatment. Probable missed LF suspicion occurred in 103 (22.2%) records. Malaria positivity was associated with missed suspicion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.30, 95% CI 2.13–13.19; p < 0.001). Interviews highlighted symptom overlap, malaria-first reasoning, treatment failure, restricted RT-PCR access, specimen-transport barriers, notification gaps and uneven refresher training. Overall, 386 (83.4%) patients recovered and 53 (11.4%) died; the case-fatality proportion among confirmed LF records was 11.4%. In this selected sample, malaria appeared to mask LF rather than establish an independent cause of mortality. Malaria confirmation should not close the LF detection pathway. Parallel assessment, timely LF specimen collection, reliable transport, effective surveillance communication and practical diagnostic algorithms may support earlier detection. References: [1]. papers.title: Assessment of Edo People Attitude Towards Lassa Fever Diseases Prevention Campaign Programme
papers.abstract: This study examines the attitudes of Edo people in Owan West Local Government Area (LGA) towards Lassa fever prevention campaigns, particularly those broadcast by KU 92.7 FM. Guided by Behaviour Theory and the Health Belief Model, the research explores how awareness and cultural beliefs influence health behaviours. Using a survey method, 398 respondents were selected through stratified and random sampling from a projected population of 112,503. Findings reveal a high level of awareness of Lassa fever, largely due to efforts by health organizations such as the NCDC, Edo State Ministry of Health, and Irrua Specialist Hospital. However, awareness does not consistently lead to preventive action, highlighting gaps in behavioural change. Trust in health professionals was found to enhance campaign effectiveness, though some skepticism persists due to misinformation and cultural beliefs. Radio emerged as a vital communication tool in rural areas, while urban populations relied more on television and social media. Cultural practices, including reliance on herbal remedies and spiritual interpretations of illness, continue to hinder adoption of preventive measures in rural communities. The study concludes that while awareness is widespread, behavioural change remains uneven. It recommends continuous public health messaging and the inclusion of traditional rulers, religious leaders, and community elders in campaign design to improve acceptance and effectiveness. Tailoring communication strategies to local contexts is essential for fostering sustained health behaviour change.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 31, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Computational study designs multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Lassa virus by October 30, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Computational study designs multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Lassa virus Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have used a purely computational, reverse vaccinology workflow to design and evaluate a multi-epitope subunit vaccine candidate against Lassa virus, the arenavirus responsible for recurrent outbreaks of Lassa fever in West Africa. The study, published open access in Discover Viruses, reports no laboratory or clinical testing; every finding is a prediction generated by bioinformatics servers, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation and immune modelling. The authors, Akeem Babatunde Sikiru, Ibrahim Shuaibu Harande and Nurulfiza Bint Mat Isa, describe the construct as a computationally validated candidate that now requires experimental validation before any claims about real-world performance can be made. The rationale for the work rests on the epidemiology of Lassa fever. The disease is endemic in Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea and Benin, with epidemiological estimates suggesting between 100,000 and 300,000 infections and approximately 5,000 deaths each year, figures the authors note are widely considered underestimates because of limited surveillance in rural, resource-constrained settings. Around 80 percent of infections are estimated to be asymptomatic or mild, but the remaining cases can progress to severe multisystem disease. The case-fatality rate among hospitalised patients is frequently cited at around 15 percent and can exceed that during major outbreaks. In pregnancy, particularly the third trimester, infection is associated with maternal mortality above 30 percent and foetal or neonatal loss in more than 80 percent of cases. No licensed vaccine exists against Lassa virus, and the authors argue that traditional development is difficult for a Biosafety Level 4 pathogen, since working with live virus requires expensive high-containment facilities. Drawing on 38 eligible studies published from January 2000 through March 2025, the review found that human behaviours and health-care conditions were the most consistently documented determinants, while the ecology of reservoir rodents and changes in the built and natural environment amplified opportunities for exposure. Lassa fever is a zoonotic viral haemorrhagic disease caused by Lassa virus and is endemic in multiple Nigerian states; the review reports that the country accounts for approximately 70% of the global disease burden. The researchers followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and searched five bibliographic databases—PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, the African Journals Online database and Google Scholar—while also consulting grey literature. They included studies investigating at least one aspect of Lassa fever risk in Nigerian endemic areas and containing empirical data. Of 612 records identified, 38 met the eligibility criteria. Methodological quality was appraised with Critical Appraisal Skills Programme and Joanna Briggs Institute checklists, and findings were synthesized thematically. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO as CRD420261436085. Among human risk factors, the studies most consistently reported open food storage, occupational exposure, poor household hygiene and nosocomial transmission in facilities without adequate infection prevention and control. The latter finding points to the role of health-care settings in allowing person-to-person transmission under deficient containment conditions. Animal evidence focused on the peri-domestic ecology of Mastomys natalensis, the rodent implicated as a reservoir of Lassa virus, with rodent density strongly correlated with human exposure. Environmental conditions—including poor housing, inadequate waste management, deforestation, climate variability and peri-urban expansion—were identified as contextual amplifiers of risk rather than isolated causes. The review’s evidence therefore supports an interconnected model in which human practices, reservoir populations and environmental change jointly shape transmission. Discover more Study Biology infection Get Health Tips health Spatial analyses in the included literature identified perennial hotspots in Edo, Ondo, Ebonyi and Plateau states, together with seasonal peaks at the end of the rainy season. The review also describes thousands of deaths during annual outbreaks, indicating that transmission has persisted despite the disease’s established endemicity. Because the evidence came from heterogeneous studies conducted across different locations and domains, the synthesis does not quantify a single population-wide effect or establish that every reported factor carries the same degree of importance. Instead, it shows that Lassa fever risk is shaped by several simultaneously operating determinants across human, animal and environmental systems. The authors conclude that controlling Lassa fever requires an integrated One Health approach rather than reliance on any one intervention. They call for strengthened infection prevention and control, improved diagnostics, community-based rodent-proofing and sanitation programmes, coordinated surveillance across humans, animals and environments, culturally tailored risk communication and sustained domestic financing. The review does not test these measures in a clinical trial, nor does it demonstrate that the combined package will reduce deaths. Its contribution is to consolidate the available empirical evidence and characterize persistent endemicity as the outcome of converging determinants, providing a rationale for coordinated surveillance and prevention across Nigeria. Drawing on 38 eligible studies published from January 2000 through March 2025, the review found that human behaviours and health-care conditions were the most consistently documented determinants, while the ecology of reservoir rodents and changes in the built and natural environment amplified opportunities for exposure. Lassa fever is a zoonotic viral haemorrhagic disease caused by Lassa virus and is endemic in multiple Nigerian states; the review reports that the country accounts for approximately 70% of the global disease burden. The researchers followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and searched five bibliographic databases—PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, the African Journals Online database and Google Scholar—while also consulting grey literature. They included studies investigating at least one aspect of Lassa fever risk in Nigerian endemic areas and containing empirical data. Of 612 records identified, 38 met the eligibility criteria. Methodological quality was appraised with Critical Appraisal Skills Programme and Joanna Briggs Institute checklists, and findings were synthesized thematically. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO as CRD420261436085. Among human risk factors, the studies most consistently reported open food storage, occupational exposure, poor household hygiene and nosocomial transmission in facilities without adequate infection prevention and control. The latter finding points to the role of health-care settings in allowing person-to-person transmission under deficient containment conditions. Animal evidence focused on the peri-domestic ecology of Mastomys natalensis, the rodent implicated as a reservoir of Lassa virus, with rodent density strongly correlated with human exposure. Environmental conditions—including poor housing, inadequate waste management, deforestation, climate variability and peri-urban expansion—were identified as contextual amplifiers of risk rather than isolated causes. The review’s evidence therefore supports an interconnected model in which human practices, reservoir populations and environmental change jointly shape transmission. Spatial analyses in the included literature identified perennial hotspots in Edo, Ondo, Ebonyi and Plateau states, together with seasonal peaks at the end of the rainy season. The review also describes thousands of deaths during annual outbreaks, indicating that transmission has persisted despite the disease’s established endemicity. Because the evidence came from heterogeneous studies conducted across different locations and domains, the synthesis does not quantify a single population-wide effect or establish that every reported factor carries the same degree of importance. Instead, it shows that Lassa fever risk is shaped by several simultaneously operating determinants across human, animal and environmental systems. The authors conclude that controlling Lassa fever requires an integrated One Health approach rather than reliance on any one intervention. They call for strengthened infection prevention and control, improved diagnostics, community-based rodent-proofing and sanitation programmes, coordinated surveillance across humans, animals and environments, culturally tailored risk communication and sustained domestic financing. The review does not test these measures in a clinical trial, nor does it demonstrate that the combined package will reduce deaths. Its contribution is to consolidate the available empirical evidence and characterize persistent endemicity as the outcome of converging determinants, providing a rationale for coordinated surveillance and prevention across Nigeria.
